cards.title: Problem 1 · Algebra
cards.stem: Let $n\ge 3$ be an integer and let $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n$ be real numbers such that $$\sum_{1\le i\lt j\le n} a_ia_j=\binom{n}{2}.$$ Prove that $$\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{a_i^2+n-1}\le 1,$$ and determine all $n$-tuples $(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ for which equality holds.

key.rationale:
Answer. Equality holds exactly for $a_1=\dots=a_n=1$ and for $a_1=\dots=a_n=-1$.

Reduction. For each $i$, $$\frac{1}{a_i^2+n-1}=\frac{1}{n-1}\left(1-\frac{a_i^2}{a_i^2+n-1}\right),$$ so the claim $\sum \frac1{a_i^2+n-1}\le 1$ is equivalent to $\frac{1}{n-1}\left(n-\sum\frac{a_i^2}{a_i^2+n-1}\right)\le 1$, i.e. to $$\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{a_i^2}{a_i^2+n-1}\ge 1.\qquad(\ast)$$

Proof of $(\ast)$. Put $s=\sum a_i$ and $Q=\sum a_i^2$. The hypothesis gives $s^2=Q+2\binom n2=Q+n(n-1)$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in Engel form (all denominators are positive), $$\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{a_i^2}{a_i^2+n-1}\ \ge\ \frac{\left(\sum a_i\right)^2}{\sum (a_i^2+n-1)}=\frac{s^2}{Q+n(n-1)}=1 .$$ This proves the inequality.

Equality. Equality in Cauchy–Schwarz holds iff $\dfrac{a_i}{a_i^2+n-1}=\lambda$ is the same for all $i$. Note $s^2=Q+n(n-1)\gt 0$, so not all $a_i$ vanish; if $\lambda=0$ every $a_i=0$, impossible. Hence $\lambda\ne0$ and every $a_i$ is a root of $\lambda t^2-t+\lambda(n-1)=0$. This quadratic has at most two roots, and if it has two roots $u\ne v$ then $uv=n-1$.

All $a_i$ equal to some $u$: then $\binom n2u^2=\binom n2$, so $u=\pm1$.

Two distinct values: say $k$ of the $a_i$ equal $u$ and $n-k$ equal $v$, $1\le k\le n-1$, $uv=n-1$. Then $$\binom n2=\sum_{i\lt j}a_ia_j=\binom k2u^2+\binom{n-k}2v^2+k(n-k)uv\ \ge\ k(n-k)(n-1)\ \ge\ (n-1)^2 ,$$ because $k(n-k)\ge n-1$ for $1\le k\le n-1$. But $(n-1)^2\gt \frac{n(n-1)}2$ for $n\ge3$, a contradiction.

Conversely, for $a_i\equiv 1$ or $a_i\equiv -1$ we have $\sum_{i\lt j}a_ia_j=\binom n2$ and $\sum\frac1{1+n-1}=1$. So equality holds exactly for these two $n$-tuples. $\blacksquare$

rubric.desc: Rewrites $\frac1{a_i^2+n-1}=\frac1{n-1}\bigl(1-\frac{a_i^2}{a_i^2+n-1}\bigr)$ (or equivalent) and reduces the problem to $\sum\frac{a_i^2}{a_i^2+n-1}\ge1$.
Uses the hypothesis in the form $(\sum a_i)^2=\sum a_i^2+n(n-1)$.
Correct application of Cauchy–Schwarz / Titu (or another complete method) that proves the inequality.
Equality condition: $a_i/(a_i^2+n-1)$ constant, with $\lambda\neq0$ justified, so each $a_i$ is a root of one quadratic.
Rules out the case of two distinct values (e.g. via $uv=n-1$ and $\sum a_ia_j\ge k(n-k)(n-1)\gt \binom n2$).
Concludes equality iff all $a_i=1$ or all $a_i=-1$, and checks these work. (Answer without proof of necessity: at most 1 of these 2.)

cards.title: Problem 2 · Number Theory
cards.stem: Find all pairs $(p,q)$ of prime numbers such that $p^2+pq+q^2$ is a perfect square.

key.rationale:
Answer. $(p,q)=(3,5)$ and $(5,3)$; indeed $9+15+25=49=7^2$.

Let $p^2+pq+q^2=k^2$ with $k$ a positive integer. Multiplying by $4$, $$4k^2=(2p+q)^2+3q^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad (2k-2p-q)(2k+2p+q)=3q^2 .$$ Put $u=2k-2p-q$ and $v=2k+2p+q$. Then $v\gt 0$, so $u\gt 0$; also $uv=3q^2$ and $$v-u=4p+2q\gt 0.$$ So $(u,v)$ is a pair of complementary divisors of $3q^2$ with $u\lt v$.

Case $q\ne3$. The divisors of $3q^2$ are $1,3,q,3q,q^2,3q^2$, and the pairs with $u\lt v$ are $(1,3q^2)$, $(3,q^2)$, $(q,3q)$.

  • $(u,v)=(q,3q)$: then $4p+2q=2q$, so $p=0$. Impossible.
  • $(u,v)=(1,3q^2)$: $4p=3q^2-2q-1=(3q+1)(q-1)$. For $q=2$ this gives $4p=7$, impossible. For odd $q$, $p=\frac{3q+1}{2}\cdot\frac{q-1}{2}$ is a product of two integers. If $q\ge5$ both factors are at least $2$, so $p$ is composite. ($q=3$ is excluded in this case.) No solutions.
  • $(u,v)=(3,q^2)$: $4p=q^2-2q-3=(q-3)(q+1)$. For $q=2$ the right side is negative. For odd $q\ge5$, $p=\frac{q-3}{2}\cdot\frac{q+1}{2}$ with $\frac{q+1}2\ge3$, so $p$ is prime only if $\frac{q-3}2=1$. Then $q=5$, $p=3$.

Case $q=3$. $3q^2=27$, and the pairs are $(1,27)$ and $(3,9)$. $(3,9)$ gives $4p+6=6$, impossible. $(1,27)$ gives $4p+6=26$, so $p=5$.

So the only solutions are $(p,q)=(3,5)$ and $(5,3)$, and both work. $\blacksquare$

rubric.desc: Obtains a useful factorisation, e.g. $(2k-2p-q)(2k+2p+q)=3q^2$ (or an equivalent one such as $(k-p)(k+p)=q(p+q)$ handled correctly).
Lists the possible divisor pairs correctly, using positivity and $u\lt v$ (with $q=3$ treated separately).
Eliminates the pair $(q,3q)$.
Case $(1,3q^2)$: shows it gives only $q=3,\ p=5$.
Case $(3,q^2)$: shows it gives only $q=5,\ p=3$.
Handles $q=2$, states the answer $(3,5),(5,3)$ and verifies it. (Answer alone with verification: 2 marks total.)

cards.title: Problem 3 · Combinatorics
cards.stim: Example for $n=4$: the triangle is cut into $16$ cells. The six shaded cells around an interior lattice point form a ring of length $6$. This is not the longest ring.

figs.cap: Triangle of side 4 divided into 16 cells; shaded: a ring of length 6.

cards.stem:
Let $n\ge 3$ be an integer. An equilateral triangle of side $n$ is divided by lines parallel to its sides into $n^2$ unit equilateral triangles, called cells.

A ring of length $k$ is a sequence $c_1,c_2,\dots,c_k$ of $k\ge3$ distinct cells such that $c_i$ and $c_{i+1}$ share a side for $i=1,\dots,k-1$, and $c_k$ and $c_1$ also share a side.

Find, in terms of $n$, the largest possible length of a ring.

You may use the isometric grid tool to draw your rings.

key.rationale:
Answer. $n(n-1)$.

Notation. Number the rows of cells $0,1,\dots,n-1$ from the top. Row $i$ contains $i+1$ upward cells $U(i,0),\dots,U(i,i)$ and $i$ downward cells $D(i,0),\dots,D(i,i-1)$, alternating $U(i,0),D(i,0),U(i,1),\dots,D(i,i-1),U(i,i)$. The three neighbours of $D(i,j)$ are $U(i,j)$, $U(i,j+1)$ (left and right) and $U(i-1,j)$ (above). In total there are $\binom{n+1}2$ upward and $\binom n2$ downward cells.

Upper bound. Every side of a cell is shared only with a cell of the opposite orientation. So the cells of a ring alternate between upward and downward, $k$ is even, and the ring contains $k/2$ distinct downward cells. Hence $k/2\le\binom n2$, i.e. $k\le n(n-1)$.

Construction. We prove by induction the statement

$(S_n)$: there is a ring through all $\binom n2$ downward cells (hence of length $n(n-1)$) in which $D(n-1,0)$ and $U(n-1,1)$ are consecutive and which does not use the corner cell $U(n-1,0)$.

$n=3$: $U(1,0),D(1,0),U(1,1),D(2,1),U(2,1),D(2,0)$ (the six cells around the interior lattice point).

$n=4$: $U(2,0),D(2,0),U(1,0),D(1,0),U(1,1),D(2,1),U(2,2),D(3,2),U(3,2),D(3,1),U(3,1),D(3,0)$.

Both are checked directly from the neighbour rule, and both satisfy the extra conditions.

Step $n\to n+2$. Let $A$ be a ring given by $(S_n)$, and add two new rows $n$ and $n+1$. These two rows contain the ring $$B:\ U(n,0),D(n,0),U(n,1),D(n,1),\dots,D(n,n-1),U(n,n),\;D(n+1,n),U(n+1,n),D(n+1,n-1),U(n+1,n-1),\dots,U(n+1,1),D(n+1,0)$$ (back to $U(n,0)$). It runs right along row $n$ and left along row $n+1$ through every downward cell of those rows; the turns use $U(n,n)\sim D(n+1,n)$ and $D(n+1,0)\sim U(n,0)$. Deleting $U(n,1)$ from $B$ leaves a path $\pi$ from $D(n,0)$ to $D(n,1)$ through all downward cells of rows $n,n+1$.

In $A$, replace the step $D(n-1,0)\to U(n-1,1)$ by $$D(n-1,0)\to U(n-1,0)\to \underbrace{D(n,0)\to\cdots\to D(n,1)}_{\pi}\to U(n-1,1).$$ The new links $D(n-1,0)\sim U(n-1,0)$, $U(n-1,0)\sim D(n,0)$ and $D(n,1)\sim U(n-1,1)$ are all sides. $U(n-1,0)$ was not used in $A$, and the cells of $\pi$ are new. So we obtain a ring in the triangle of side $n+2$ through all its downward cells. It still contains the consecutive pair $D(n+1,0),U(n+1,1)$ (from $\pi$) and does not use $U(n+1,0)$. This proves $(S_{n+2})$. From the bases $n=3,4$ we get $(S_n)$ for every $n\ge3$.

So the maximum is exactly $n(n-1)$. $\blacksquare$

rubric.desc: Observes that cells sharing a side have opposite orientations, so a ring alternates up/down.
Concludes $k\le 2\binom n2=n(n-1)$ (counts downward cells correctly).
Correct answer, with valid rings for small cases (e.g. $n=3$ and $n=4$).
A general construction of a ring of length $n(n-1)$ for every $n\ge3$ (inductive splicing or explicit). A construction that works for only one parity of $n$, or has a fixable gap: up to 5.
Checks the construction carefully (adjacency, distinctness, every downward cell used).

cards.title: Problem 4 · Geometry

figs.cap: The configuration of Problem 4 (Γ is the circumcircle). D is the foot of the altitude from A.

cards.stem:
Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB\lt AC$, circumcircle $\Gamma$ and orthocentre $H$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. The line through $H$ perpendicular to $AM$ meets line $BC$ at $T$. The line $AT$ meets $\Gamma$ again at $P\neq A$.

Prove that $P$, $H$, $M$ are collinear.

key.rationale:
$T$ exists. The line through $H$ perpendicular to $AM$ is parallel to $BC$ only if $AM\perp BC$, i.e. only if $AB=AC$. Since $AB\lt AC$, $T$ is well defined.

Step 1: $MH\perp AT$. In triangle $ATM$, the line $AH$ is perpendicular to $BC=TM$, and the line $TH$ is perpendicular to $AM$. So $H$ lies on two altitudes of triangle $ATM$ and is its orthocentre. Hence $MH\perp AT$. Let $Q$ be the intersection of lines $MH$ and $AT$. Then $Q$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to line $MH$. (Line $MH$ is well defined since $H e M$, and $A otin MH$: otherwise $A,H,M$ would be collinear, so $AM\perp BC$ and $AB=AC$.) In particular $Q eq A$.

Step 2: the antipode. Let $A'$ be the point of $\Gamma$ diametrically opposite to $A$. Then $A'C\perp AC$ and $BH\perp AC$, so $A'C\parallel BH$. Similarly $A'B\parallel CH$. So $BHCA'$ is a parallelogram, its diagonals bisect each other, and $M$ is the midpoint of $HA'$. Hence line $MH$ passes through $A'$.

Step 3. The line $A'H$ passes through the interior point $H$, so it meets $\Gamma$ at a second point $Q' e A'$. Since $AA'$ is a diameter, $\angle AQ'A'=90^\circ$, i.e. $AQ'\perp$ line $A'H=$ line $MH$. (Here $Q' e A$ because $A otin MH$; also $H e M$, since otherwise $M$ would lie on the altitude from $A$ and $AB=AC$.) So $Q'$ is also the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to line $MH$, and therefore $Q'=Q$.

Conclusion. $Q$ lies on $\Gamma$, on line $AT$, and $Q e A$. So $Q$ is the second intersection $P$ of $AT$ with $\Gamma$. Since $Q$ lies on $MH$, the points $P,H,M$ are collinear. (As a by-product, $\angle APH=90^\circ$.) $ lacksquare$

rubric.desc: Notes that $T$ exists because $AB\ne AC$.
Shows $H$ is the orthocentre of triangle $ATM$, hence $MH\perp AT$.
Shows that line $MH$ passes through the antipode $A'$ of $A$ (parallelogram $BHCA'$, or reflection of $H$ in $M$).
Shows that the second intersection of line $A'H$ with $\Gamma$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $MH$ (right angle on the diameter).
Identifies this point with $P$, with non-degeneracy handled ($A\notin MH$, $Q\ne A$), and concludes. A complete alternative proof (coordinates, complex numbers, inversion) earns full marks.
